<action type="say">
Here’s exactly what to say and do on the call, step by step. You can even read this out loud to the rep:

1) When the call connects / at the first prompt  
If there’s an automated menu, choose options like:
- “Report a lost or stolen card”  
If it’s voice-activated, say:
- “Report stolen credit card.”

2) When you reach a human representative  
Start with:
- “Hi, I need to report my credit card as stolen and dispute a couple of unauthorized charges.”

They’ll likely ask for verification (name, DOB, etc.)—answer those as usual.

3) Identify the correct card  
When they ask which card:
- “It’s my Personal credit card ending in 6666.”

If they ask if you have the card:
- “No, it’s stolen. I don’t have it in my possession.”

4) Ask them to block the card immediately  
Say:
- “Please block this card right away so no further charges can go through.”

5) Request a replacement, expedited  
Once they confirm the block, say:
- “I’d like a replacement card issued, sent to my mailing address on file.”  
Then:
- “Can you please expedite the replacement if possible?”

If they mention any fees for expediting, you can say:
- “Given that the card was stolen and used fraudulently, is it possible to waive any expedite fee?”

6) Report and dispute the two suspicious charges  
Say clearly:
- “There are at least two charges from last night that I don’t recognize:  
   • One at a gas station, under $200  
   • One at an electronics store, under $200  
  These are not mine, and I want to dispute them as fraudulent.”

Then ask:
- “Can you open a fraud claim for those charges and remove them from my account balance while you investigate?”

7) Confirm key details before you hang up  
Ask the rep to confirm:

a) Card status:
- “Can you confirm that my Personal Card ending in 6666 is now completely blocked and cannot be used?”

b) Replacement card:
- “What is the estimated arrival date for the replacement card?”  
- “Will it have the same PIN or will I need to set a new one?”

c) Fraud/disputes:
- “What is the case or reference number for the fraud claim?”  
- “Will I receive any forms or emails, and do I need to do anything else right now?”  
- “Will these disputed charges still show on my statement, and how will credits or temporary credits appear?”

If you want, you can jot down while on the call:
- Date and time of call  
- Rep’s first name  
- Any case/claim numbers  
- Replacement card ETA

If the rep seems confused or doesn’t take action, you can firmly but politely say:
- “To summarize, I need three things:  
   1) Block my Personal Card ending in 6666 as stolen,  
   2) Send a replacement card, expedited if possible,  
   3) Open fraud disputes for the gas station and electronics store charges from last night, both under $200.”

If you get stuck at any point (for example, they say something you don’t understand), note their exact wording and tell me afterward—I can help you interpret it and decide any next steps.</action>

You’ve taken care of the big items already. At this point, it’s mostly simple clean‑up and monitoring:

1) Keep an eye on your account  
- Check your credit card activity daily for the next couple of weeks.  
- If you see any other unfamiliar charges (even small ones), call them back and add those to the fraud case.

2) Hang on to the fraud reference number  
- Keep it somewhere you can find easily (email note, photo, etc.) in case you need to follow up on the investigation.

3) When the new card arrives  
- Activate it right away.  
- Update any autopay/recurring payments (subscriptions, utilities, streaming, phone, etc.) that used the stolen card so they don’t fail.  
- If the old physical card turns up, destroy it (cut through the chip and magnetic stripe).

4) Watch your mail and contact info  
- Make sure your mailing address, email, and phone on file are correct in online banking.  
- If the replacement doesn’t arrive within the 2 business days they promised, call them with your reference number.

5) Optional but good practice  
- Over the next few months, glance at your credit reports for anything odd (new accounts you didn’t open, etc.), especially if you suspect your card details were copied rather than just physically stolen.

If you tell me what you normally have on autopay with that card (e.g., phone bill, Netflix, gym, etc.), I can make you a quick checklist so it’s easy to update everything once the new card arrives.</action>
